original_value: We investigate cybersecurity toolkits, collections of public facing materials intended to help users achieve security online. Through a qualitative analysis of 41 online toolkits, we present a set of key design dimensions: agentive scale (who is responsible for security), achievability (can security be achieved), and interventional stage (when are security measures taken). Recognizing toolkits as socially and culturally situated, we surface ways in which toolkits construct security as a value and, in so doing, how they construct people as (in)secure users. We center the notion of differential vulnerabilities, an understanding of security that recognizes safety as socially contingent, adversaries as unstable figures, and risk as differentially applied based on markers of relational position (e.g. class, race, religion, gender, geography, experience). We argue that differential vulnerabilities provides a key design concern in future security resources, and a critical concept for security discourses.

result.paraphrase: We examine cybersecurity toolkits—collections of public-facing materials meant to help people stay secure online. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of 41 online toolkits, we identify three key design dimensions: agentive scale (who bears responsibility for security), achievability (whether security can be achieved), and interventional stage (when security measures are taken). Treating toolkits as socially and culturally situated, we show how they frame security as a value and, in doing so, how they cast people as (in)secure users. We foreground differential vulnerabilities, a view of security that understands safety as socially contingent, adversaries as unstable figures, and risk as unevenly assigned according to markers of relational position such as class, race, religion, gender, geography, and experience. We contend that differential vulnerabilities should be a central design concern for future security resources and a critical concept in security discourse.
